name: NVIDIA Enterprise Marketplace / Partner Network (NPN) as an acquisition channel
region: Worldwide; directory filterable by country (the SuperPOD specialization view is location=US in NVIDIA's own example link)
notes:
QUOTE-ONLY by construction. Recorded separately from nvidia-dgx-direct because this is the ROUTING artefact rather than the hardware: marketplace.nvidia.com is where an enterprise actually finds the specific reseller, integrator or CSP that will sell it to them, and NVIDIA links to it as the 'Find a Partner' destination from the DGX page. Partner categories listed are Cloud Service Providers and Partner Servers, plus specializations that map to real buying needs (SuperPOD deployment expertise, DGX-Ready Lifecycle Management, colocation). Two consequences for anyone sourcing hardware: (1) the transacting legal entity is the partner, so warranty, support SLA and liability sit with them, not NVIDIA; (2) the directory is the practical place to see how many resellers a given country actually has, which is a real constraint on regional tenders. No public price anywhere on the directory. EXPORT CONTROLLED (true). Regime: US BIS advanced-computing export controls (the Oct 2023 interim final rule, 88 FR 73458 - source sup-buy-bis-2023-advanced-computing-controls), which put datacenter accelerators under ECCN 3A090/4A090, added the advanced-computing Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rule, and extended Regional Stability (RS) controls to Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5. For items destined to Macau or Country Group D:5 the rule applies a PRESUMPTION OF DENIAL; other RS destinations get a presumption of approval. Practical effect: which accelerator you can legally be sold, and which SKU counts as compliant, is set by destination and end user - not by the channel.

 LEAD TIME, recorded as an EXPLICIT NEGATIVE with a bound rather than a fabricated week count. NVIDIA publishes no lead time in weeks on any page, and this record is quote-only, so lead_time_weeks stays null: any number would be invented. What CAN be said from a primary source is the shape of the horizon. NVIDIA's FY2026 Form 10-K (filed 2026-02-25, source spl-nvda-10k-fy2026-supply-commitments) reports outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply and capacity obligations of $95.2 BILLION as of 2026-01-25, 'of which substantially all will be paid through fiscal year 2027', against $21.4 billion of consolidated inventories. A forward book of that size against roughly one year of payments implies an order horizon on the order of several quarters, so plan in quarters rather than weeks. Two further reasons the true lead time is longer than any published figure: the 10-K states NVIDIA 'may place non-cancellable inventory orders for certain product components IN ADVANCE OF OUR HISTORICAL LEAD TIMES, pay premiums, or provide deposits to secure future supply and capacity' - the vendor itself buys beyond its own lead times - and supply is concentrated in TSMC/Samsung wafers, SK Hynix/Micron/Samsung memory, CoWoS packaging and Hon Hai/Wistron/Fabrinet assembly. Corroborating but NOT a substitute: CDW, one of the few distributors that prints a lead time, shows '4-6+ Weeks' for the NVIDIA DGX B200 8x180GB server (source spl-cdw-published-lead-times-gpu-2026-10) - that is CDW's inbound window on one SKU, an open-ended range, and it contradicts the multi-quarter horizon above, which is precisely why a distributor's number must not be read as the OEM's. Re-verify each quarter against a fresh 10-Q.
